content: Most of the cohort studies were conducted in high-income countries, with six studies originating from lowand middle-income countries (LMICs). The three case-control studies included 469 women and 871 neonates. The gestational age range was 28 to 36 weeks in two studies and 26 to 32 weeks in the third study. These studies used different administration-to-birth intervals. Two case-control studies were conducted in high-income countries (Israel and the USA), while one was conducted in Iran (an LMIC). Maternal Outcomes: Maternal Infectious Morbidity: Evidence regarding the relationship between corticosteroid administration-to-birth intervals and chorioamnionitis was inconsistent for intervals longer than 7 days. Some studies reported an increased risk, while others found no difference compared to placebo or no treatment (low to moderate risk of bias, 3 studies, at least 3186 women). For intervals shorter than 24 hours, studies consistently reported no difference (low to moderate risk of bias, 3 studies, at least 2881 women). Similarly, no difference was observed for intervals of 2–7 days (moderate risk of bias, 2 studies, 3017 women). One study did not report the number of women included. Infant Outcomes: Fetal and Neonatal Death: Evidence on corticosteroid administration-to-birth intervals and perinatal death was limited. One study (serious risk of bias, 460 infants) found reduced odds of perinatal mortality with antenatal corticosteroids administered at intervals longer than 48 hours compared to no treatment, but not for intervals shorter than 48 hours. Two other studies did not detect differences in perinatal mortality for intervals shorter than 7 days or longer than 7 days. Evidence on neonatal death was inconsistent across most time intervals. Studies variably reported reduced odds, increased odds, or no difference for intervals shorter than 24 hours (critical to low risk of bias, 10 studies, 10,703 infants). For intervals of 2–7 days, studies reported no difference or reduced odds (serious to moderate risk of bias, 4 studies, 4058 infants). For intervals longer than 7 days, studies reported no difference or reduced odds (serious to low risk of bias, 4 studies, 6220 neonates). However, reduced odds of neonatal death were consistently reported for intervals of 1–7 days (critical to low risk of bias, 3 studies, 4989 women). Severe Neonatal Morbidity: Evidence on corticosteroid administration-to-birth intervals and respiratory distress syndrome was inconsistent. Observational studies reported no differences for intervals shorter than 24 hours (critical to moderate risk of bias, 5 studies, 1664 infants). For intervals of 2–7 days, studies reported reduced odds or no difference (serious to moderate risk of bias, 3 studies, 1270 infants). For intervals longer than 7 days, studies reported reduced odds or no difference (moderate risk of bias, 2 studies, 1016 infants). Intraventricular Hemorrhage: Evidence was consistent for some time intervals. Observational studies reported reduced odds of intraventricular hemorrhage for intervals of 1–7 days (critical to low risk of bias, 4 studies, 1925 infants) and longer than 7 days (low to moderate risk of bias, 4 studies, 4461 infants). For intervals shorter than 24 hours, studies reported reduced odds or no difference (low to moderate risk of bias, 5 studies, 4264 infants). For intervals of 2–7 days, studies reported reduced odds or no difference (moderate risk of bias, 2 studies, 3097 infants). Necrotizing Enterocolitis: Evidence was inconsistent. Four studies reported no differences for any time interval (critical to moderate risk of bias, 1577 infants). One study found increased odds compared to no treatment for intervals longer than 7 days (low risk of bias, 169 infants). Chronic Lung Disease: Evidence was inconsistent for some time intervals. Reduced odds or no difference were reported for intervals of 2–7 days (moderate to serious risk of bias, 2 studies, 2803 infants) and longer than 7 days (low to moderate risk of bias, 2 studies, 919 infants). No difference was reported for intervals shorter than 24 hours (low to moderate risk of bias, 3 studies, 2881 infants) and 1–7 days (low risk of bias, 1 study, 169 infants). Neonatal Sepsis: Evidence was inconsistent. Studies found both increased odds and no differences when compared to no treatment for intervals of 2–7 days (serious to moderate risk of bias, 4 studies, 3819 infants) and longer than 7 days (low to moderate risk of bias, 4 studies, 3734 infants). No differences were reported for intervals shorter than 24 hours (low to moderate risk of bias, 3 studies, 3266 infants) or 1–7 days (low risk of bias, 1 study, 169 infants). Additional Data: Statistical Modeling: A systematic review included an observational study from 11 European countries (4594 singleton infants, gestational ages 24–31 weeks, without severe anomalies). This study showed that neonatal mortality was immediately reduced within the first 24 hours after corticosteroid administration, including within the first 6 hours. A 50% risk reduction in neonatal death was observed at 18–36 hours. Benefits persisted up to 5 weeks post-administration, though confidence intervals crossed the line of no effect at approximately 24–25 days after administration. Secondary Analysis of the ACTION-1 Trial: Data from a secondary analysis of an included trial (WHO, unpublished) indicated that longer administration-to-birth intervals were consistently more beneficial, regardless of gestational age. Values and Preferences: Women and their families value the benefits of antenatal corticosteroids but prefer their use only when necessary and in the context of a positive relationship with healthcare providers. They prefer clear information about treatment options and adequate time for shared decision-making. Most healthcare providers believe the benefits of antenatal corticosteroids outweigh the risks, though some express concerns about safety in specific clinical situations. Resource Considerations: Antenatal corticosteroids are relatively inexpensive, easy to administer, and widely available in at least one preparation. However, implementation requires skilled health personnel to identify preterm labor, administer intramuscular injections, and monitor care. Accurate gestational age estimation requires personnel trained in obstetric ultrasound. Preterm infants may require additional specialist care. Training for health personnel is essential for safe and effective administration. Additional training may be needed in settings where antenatal corticosteroids are not yet available. Costs include intramuscular administration supplies (needles, syringes, antiseptic solution, swabs, gloves, sharps disposal) and potential additional investigations (blood tests, urinalysis, fetal heart monitoring). Preterm infants often require additional care, such as oxygen or respiratory support, feeding support, warmth, hygiene measures, infection management, or neonatal intensive care. Equity: Preterm birth and its adverse consequences disproportionately affect women and newborns in disadvantaged circumstances, such as those living in rural areas, with limited education, or with poor access to quality antenatal and intrapartum care. Antenatal corticosteroids, being relatively inexpensive and widely available, can increase equity by providing protection to these populations. Acceptability: Providers may be uncertain about the benefits and risks of antenatal corticosteroids and when to use them. Acceptability can be improved by providing high-quality evidence on effectiveness and safety, clear guidelines, training to improve administration skills, and promoting a multidisciplinary approach with defined roles and responsibilities. Feasibility: Feasibility may be impacted by varying levels of provider knowledge, the unpredictability of preterm birth, and high staff workloads. Correct use can be improved through education, clear clinical protocols, and ensuring facilities are well-stocked. Pre-referral first-dose administration in lower-level facilities may face challenges such as identifying preterm labor, limited knowledge about pre-referral dosing, and transportation issues.
